title: Learning algorithms that extrapolate beyond training lengths
open: Identify training distributions and inductive biases that produce algorithms whose correctness persists at substantially greater input lengths. Require performance curves and, where possible, guarantees beyond the lengths used for training and model selection.
status: Systematic-generalization failures have been studied since at least 2017; scratchpads provide a useful partial mechanism. Success on selected arithmetic tasks does not establish general length extrapolation.
why: Supports reliable reasoning over larger programs, documents, graphs, and proofs.
key_works: Lake and Baroni, 2017/2018, *Generalization without systematicity*, arXiv:1711.00350; Nye et al., 2021, *Show Your Work*, arXiv:2112.00114.

title: Predicting grokking before generalization occurs
open: Predict whether, when, and on which distributions a memorizing network will transition to generalization, using measurements available before that transition. The predictor should transfer across tasks, optimizers, architectures, and training scales.
status: Grokking was documented in 2022 on small algorithmic datasets. Explaining individual examples is weaker than forecasting transition times and distinguishing eventual generalization from permanent overfitting.
why: Could avoid wasted training and reveal which internal structures support abstraction.
key_works: Power et al., 2022, *Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets*, arXiv:2201.02177.

title: Deployment-relevant generalization certificates
open: Produce computable generalization bounds that meaningfully predict downstream error, including important distribution shifts, for practically trained LLMs. Bounds should distinguish better from worse models rather than merely fall below a trivial ceiling.
status: Non-vacuous bounds already exist: 2023 work addressed large compressed models, and 2024 token-level bounds reached compressed LLaMA2-70B. The remaining target is tightness and deployment relevance, not the existence of any non-vacuous bound.
why: Provides a mathematical complement to benchmark-based assurance.
key_works: Lotfi et al., 2023, *Non-Vacuous Generalization Bounds for Large Language Models*, arXiv:2312.17173; Lotfi et al., 2024, *Unlocking Tokens as Data Points for Generalization Bounds on Larger Language Models*, arXiv:2407.18158.

title: Distinguishing genuine capability transitions from measurement artifacts
open: Develop tests that distinguish a real qualitative change in learned computation from thresholding, discontinuous scoring, contamination, or sparse sampling of model sizes. Specify what observations would falsify an emergence claim.
status: The 2023 “mirage” analysis demonstrated that some apparent emergence depends on metric choice. It does not establish that every qualitative transition is an artifact.
why: Improves scaling forecasts and prevents misleading capability narratives.
key_works: Schaeffer, Miranda, and Koyejo, 2023, *Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?*, arXiv:2304.15004; Kaplan et al., 2020, *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*, arXiv:2001.08361.

title: Scaling-law transfer across domains
subfield: Scaling laws, optimization, and resource allocation
open: Predict downstream capability from small experiments when the target domain, data mixture, or evaluation distribution differs substantially from the fitted scaling regime. Predictions should include calibrated extrapolation uncertainty.
status: Power-law descriptions date to 2020; subsequent work tests overtraining and downstream-task scaling. Reliable transfer to new domains and architectures is a stronger requirement than interpolation within a training family.
why: Reduces expensive failed training programs.
key_works: Kaplan et al., 2020, *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*, arXiv:2001.08361; Gadre et al., 2024, *Language models scale reliably with over-training and on downstream tasks*, arXiv:2403.08540.

title: Hyperparameter transfer across architectural changes
subfield: Scaling laws, optimization, and resource allocation
open: Transfer learning rates, initialization, regularization, and optimizer settings across simultaneous changes in width, depth, sequence length, precision, and architecture. Quantify where transfer fails and supply inexpensive corrective measurements.
status: μP demonstrated valuable zero-shot transfer across model widths in 2022. A general transfer rule covering all of these changes is a substantially stronger target.
why: Cuts the cost and instability of scaling experiments.
key_works: Yang et al., 2022, *Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer*, arXiv:2203.03466.

title: Tenfold reduction in unique training-data requirements
subfield: Scaling laws, optimization, and resource allocation
open: Match a preregistered baseline’s broad, contamination-controlled performance using at most one-tenth as much unique training data, without hiding equivalent information in teachers or synthetic-data generators.
status: Data-mixture optimization and large-scale curation provide measurable improvements. A broad tenfold information-efficiency improvement under explicit information accounting is the proposed moonshot.
why: Makes capable models feasible for domains and languages with scarce data.
key_works: Xie et al., 2023, *DoReMi*, arXiv:2305.10429; Penedo et al., 2024, *The FineWeb Datasets*, arXiv:2406.17557.

title: Preserving rare tails during synthetic augmentation
subfield: Training data, provenance, and synthetic-data dynamics
open: Preserve rare but important facts, dialects, failure cases, and decision boundaries across repeated synthetic augmentation. Demonstrate tail preservation separately from average benchmark performance.
status: Recursive-training studies identify distributional degradation, while accumulation mitigates some collapse regimes. Tail-specific guarantees and realistic rare-event evaluations remain distinct targets.
why: Prevents apparently improving models from becoming less useful to uncommon users and cases.
key_works: Shumailov et al., 2023, *The Curse of Recursion*, arXiv:2305.17493; Gerstgrasser et al., 2024, *Is Model Collapse Inevitable?*, arXiv:2404.01413.

title: Adaptive byte-level modeling without language penalties
open: Learn variable-rate segmentation that preserves multilingual quality, handles corrupted or novel strings, and allocates computation according to information content rather than tokenizer accidents.
status: Byte Latent Transformer explored dynamic byte patching at scales up to 8 billion parameters in 2024. Robustness, efficiency, and language equity must still be jointly demonstrated.
why: Reduces tokenizer brittleness and uneven costs across writing systems.
key_works: Pagnoni et al., 2024, *Byte Latent Transformer: Patches Scale Better Than Tokens*, arXiv:2412.09871; Petrov et al., 2023, *Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages*, arXiv:2305.15425.

title: Optimal stopping for test-time reasoning
open: Stop reasoning when expected improvement no longer justifies added latency, expense, or risk. Estimate this online without knowing the correct answer or using an oracle difficulty label.
status: Test-time compute allocation has demonstrated gains since 2024. A transferable stopping policy with reliable uncertainty remains a distinct target.
why: Avoids both premature answers and expensive unproductive deliberation.
key_works: Snell et al., 2024, *Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters*, arXiv:2408.03314.

title: Position-invariant use of relevant context
open: Preserve answer quality when relevant evidence moves within a long context, while holding content and distractors constant. Extend evaluation beyond single-needle retrieval to multi-evidence reasoning.
status: “Lost in the Middle” documented position sensitivity in 2023. Longer advertised context windows do not themselves establish position-invariant reasoning.
why: Makes document order less likely to determine correctness.
key_works: Liu et al., 2023, *Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts*, arXiv:2307.03172; Bai et al., 2023, *LongBench*, arXiv:2308.14508.

title: Revising memories without losing historical truth
open: Update beliefs when facts change or earlier information is corrected, while retaining when each statement was believed and why. Avoid both stale answers and rewriting history.
status: LongMemEval includes knowledge-update and temporal-reasoning challenges. A robust memory model must distinguish correction, change, contradiction, and uncertainty.
why: Supports dependable long-term assistance and auditability.
key_works: Wu et al., 2024, *LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory*, arXiv:2410.10813.

title: Precise memory deletion without collateral forgetting
open: Remove a specified fact or experience from retrievable and parametric memory while preserving unrelated knowledge. Verify deletion against paraphrases, inference, and later updates.
status: ROME and MEMIT demonstrate targeted editing; TOFU benchmarks unlearning. Editing an answer and eliminating recoverable information are not equivalent.
why: Supports user corrections, privacy requests, and removal of poisoned memories.
key_works: Meng et al., 2022, *Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT*, arXiv:2202.05262; Maini et al., 2024, *TOFU*, arXiv:2401.06121.

title: Realistic longitudinal memory evaluation
open: Build consented, longitudinal evaluations containing forgotten details, changed preferences, contradictory reports, multiple people, and meaningful consequences for errors. Prevent answers from being recoverable through superficial lexical cues.
status: LoCoMo and LongMemEval are concrete 2024 baselines. Longer, more representative and privacy-preserving evaluations remain an expansion target.
why: Separates genuine long-term assistance from benchmark-specific retrieval tricks.
key_works: Maharana et al., 2024, *Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents*, arXiv:2402.17753; Wu et al., 2024, *LongMemEval*, arXiv:2410.10813.

title: Out-of-distribution abstention with useful coverage
open: Detect unfamiliar situations and abstain at a controlled error rate without refusing most useful work. Evaluate shifts not represented in the abstention system’s development data.
status: Open-set recognition and LLM confidence estimation supply partial methods. Useful coverage under genuinely novel shifts is stronger than thresholding a familiar benchmark.
why: Enables graceful failure when a model encounters conditions outside its competence.
key_works: Bendale and Boult, 2015/2016, *Towards Open Set Deep Networks*, arXiv:1511.06233; Kadavath et al., 2022, *Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know*, arXiv:2207.05221.

title: Predicting real deployment outcomes from benchmarks
open: Determine which benchmark measurements predict error rates, productivity, user benefit, and harm in actual deployments. Validate the mapping prospectively across organizations and model updates.
status: HELM broadens evaluation dimensions, while realistic agent benchmarks move closer to workflows. External validity still requires field validation rather than assumed transfer.
why: Stops organizations from optimizing scores that do not predict useful outcomes.
key_works: Liang et al., 2022, *Holistic Evaluation of Language Models*, arXiv:2211.09110; Yao et al., 2024, *τ-bench*, arXiv:2406.12045.

title: Metamorphic tests for semantic invariance
open: Generate transformations that should preserve an answer or change it in a precisely known way, then detect violations. Cover paraphrase, units, entity renaming, document order, and irrelevant context.
status: Compositional and long-context benchmarks expose selected invariance failures. A systematic transformation library with validated semantic preservation remains a useful missing infrastructure.
why: Finds brittle behavior without requiring a new gold answer for every example.
key_works: Hsieh et al., 2023, *SugarCrepe*, arXiv:2306.14610; Liu et al., 2023, *Lost in the Middle*, arXiv:2307.03172.

title: Identifiability of learned interpretability features
open: Determine when different feature decompositions represent the same underlying computation and when they imply incompatible explanations. Supply uncertainty or equivalence classes rather than treating one dictionary as canonical.
status: Sparse-autoencoder research establishes useful decompositions and scaling methods. Nonuniqueness and dependence on training choices remain important residual questions.
why: Makes feature-level scientific claims reproducible.
key_works: Cunningham et al., 2023, *Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features*, arXiv:2309.08600; Gao et al., 2024, *Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders*, arXiv:2406.04093.

title: Faithful natural-language explanations
open: Generate explanations whose stated reasons correspond to factors that actually caused the answer. Distinguish retrospective rationalization from a faithful account using interventions.
status: 2023 studies demonstrated unfaithful chain-of-thought explanations and proposed tests. Fluent reasoning remains insufficient evidence of faithfulness.
why: Makes explanations useful for debugging and justified trust.
key_works: Turpin et al., 2023, *Language Models Don’t Always Say What They Think*, arXiv:2305.04388; Lanham et al., 2023, *Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning*, arXiv:2307.13702.

title: Indirect prompt-injection resistance with preserved utility
open: Prevent untrusted documents, webpages, messages, and tool outputs from changing an agent’s authorized goals or permissions. Demonstrate resistance under adaptive attacks while retaining useful document processing.
status: Indirect injection was documented in 2023; AgentDojo and CaMeL provide evaluation and architectural defenses. Utility-preserving coverage across heterogeneous applications remains broader.
why: Protects agents that must read adversarially supplied information.
key_works: Greshake et al., 2023, *Not what you’ve signed up for*, arXiv:2302.12173; Debenedetti et al., 2025, *Defeating Prompt Injections by Design*, arXiv:2503.18813.

title: Valid membership-inference audits
open: Measure whether a model reveals training membership while controlling for distribution mismatch, duplicates, and public availability. Report false-positive rates suitable for consequential claims.
status: Membership inference has a foundational 2016–2017 literature; LLM data extraction provides a related but different privacy signal.
why: Prevents both overlooked privacy leakage and unsupported accusations of training use.
key_works: Shokri et al., 2016/2017, *Membership Inference Attacks against Machine Learning Models*, arXiv:1610.05820; Carlini et al., 2020/2021, *Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models*, arXiv:2012.07805.

title: Certified unlearning for practically trained LLMs
open: Remove specified training contributions with a certificate meaningfully related to retraining without those contributions. Preserve utility and avoid requiring full retraining for every request.
status: Certified removal exists for restricted model classes; TOFU supplies an LLM unlearning benchmark. Behavioral suppression alone is not a certified removal result.
why: Makes deletion requests technically meaningful.
key_works: Guo et al., 2019/2020, *Certified Data Removal from Machine Learning Models*, arXiv:1911.03030; Maini et al., 2024, *TOFU*, arXiv:2401.06121.

title: Unlearning that survives later training
open: Ensure removed information does not reappear after unrelated fine-tuning, model merging, memory retrieval, or exposure to correlated examples. Define when relearning from genuinely new authorized data is permissible.
status: Unlearning benchmarks and large-scale editing methods address immediate behavior. Durability across a model’s subsequent lifecycle is an additional requirement.
why: Prevents deletion from being a temporary surface effect.
key_works: Maini et al., 2024, *TOFU*, arXiv:2401.06121; Meng et al., 2022/2023, *Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer*, arXiv:2210.07229.

title: Prompt revocation of delegated authority
subfield: Durable agent infrastructure and distributed execution
open: Propagate permission revocation to running agents, queued actions, cached credentials, and delegated subagents with explicit latency and failure guarantees.
status: Agent security architectures constrain execution, but revocation across persistent distributed work adds lifecycle requirements beyond initial authorization.
why: Ensures users can genuinely withdraw access and stop future effects.
key_works: Debenedetti et al., 2025, *Defeating Prompt Injections by Design*, arXiv:2503.18813; Gao et al., 2024, *AgentScope*, arXiv:2402.14034.

title: Diversity that actually reduces correlated agent errors
open: Construct agent ensembles whose disagreements reflect independent evidence or computation rather than superficial persona variation. Measure reduction in correlated failures at matched total cost.
status: Multi-agent frameworks enable ensembles, but failure analysis shows coordination and shared-error problems. More agents need not provide independent verification.
why: Makes redundancy a real reliability mechanism.
key_works: Wu et al., 2023, *AutoGen*, arXiv:2308.08155; Cemri et al., 2025, *Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?*, arXiv:2503.13657.

title: Reliable visual attribute and relation binding
open: Correctly bind attributes, actions, and relations to the right entities in crowded or compositionally novel scenes. Resist language-only shortcuts.
status: Winoground and SugarCrepe provide concrete compositional evaluations from 2022–2023. Strong aggregate vision-language scores do not imply robust binding.
why: Supports precise visual reasoning rather than bag-of-concepts recognition.
key_works: Thrush et al., 2022, *Winoground*, arXiv:2204.03162; Hsieh et al., 2023, *SugarCrepe*, arXiv:2306.14610.

title: Transfer to genuinely new robot embodiments
open: Transfer skills to robots with different kinematics, sensors, grippers, and action spaces using minimal new data. Separate embodiment transfer from retraining on a closely related platform.
status: Open X-Embodiment and Octo demonstrate cross-robot data and generalist policies. Broad, low-data transfer to unseen embodiments remains a stronger goal.
why: Avoids rebuilding the learning stack for every robot.
key_works: Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2023, *Open X-Embodiment*, arXiv:2310.08864; Octo Model Team, 2024, *Octo*, arXiv:2405.12213.

title: Off-policy evaluation with hidden confounding
subfield: Reinforcement learning, continual learning, and open-ended adaptation
open: Estimate a new policy’s consequences from observational logs when action selection depends on unrecorded information. Return valid uncertainty or partial-identification bounds when point estimates are unjustified.
status: Offline RL formalizes evaluation from logged experience; real operational data can violate the assumptions needed for ordinary estimators.
why: Prevents unsafe policy deployment based on biased retrospective estimates.
key_works: Levine et al., 2020, *Offline Reinforcement Learning*, arXiv:2005.01643; Chaney et al., 2017/2018, *How Algorithmic Confounding in Recommendation Systems Increases Homogeneity and Decreases Utility*, arXiv:1710.11214.

title: Measuring AI incidents without denominator blindness
open: Estimate incident rates and severity with meaningful exposure denominators, consistent classifications, and reporting-bias correction. Avoid interpreting raw report counts as population risk.
status: The AI Incident Database established an important cataloging approach in 2020–2021. Catalogs alone do not identify incidence rates.
why: Makes safety trends and intervention effectiveness measurable.
key_works: McGregor, 2020/2021, *Preventing Repeated Real World AI Failures by Cataloging Incidents: The AI Incident Database*, arXiv:2011.08512.

title: Discriminating tests for AI consciousness and welfare relevance
open: Develop empirically discriminating methods for evaluating theories of consciousness in artificial systems, while distinguishing verbal self-report, functional indicators, and moral uncertainty.
status: Butlin et al. synthesized theory-derived indicators in 2023. There is no implication that present systems are conscious, nor a settled test that resolves the question.
why: Informs cautious decisions about potentially welfare-relevant future systems.
key_works: Butlin et al., 2023, *Consciousness in Artificial Intelligence: Insights from the Science of Consciousness*, arXiv:2308.08708.
